# @jpisgeek/hyperv

A Hyper-V host, read over SSH and acted on deliberately. `discover` is read-only
and covers the host's capacity, one record per virtual machine, and one per
virtual switch. Checkpoints are recorded by the checkpoint methods rather than
by `discover`, so a checkpoint record reflects a deliberate act on that VM and
not a periodic sweep. Lifecycle methods mutate, and each destructive one makes
the caller name what it is about to destroy. There is no REST or JSON-RPC
surface for Hyper-V, so PowerShell is the API and SSH is how it is reached.

**Version** `2026.08.29.1` · **License** MIT · **Source**
https://github.com/jpisgeek/slog-bog/tree/main/hyperv

## Install

```
swamp extension pull @jpisgeek/hyperv
```

## `@jpisgeek/hyperv`

### Arguments

| argument     | type    | required | default | description                                                                                                                 |
| ------------ | ------- | -------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `host`       | string  | yes      |         | Address of the Hyper-V host's SSH server. Source it from a vault expression so no machine identity lands in a tracked file. |
| `user`       | string  | yes      |         | Login user for SSH. Also vault-sourced; on Windows this is frequently an account whose name differs from the fleet default. |
| `port`       | integer | no       | `22`    |                                                                                                                             |
| `timeoutSec` | integer | no       | `30`    |                                                                                                                             |

### Methods

#### `discover`

Read-only sweep of the Hyper-V host, its VMs, and its virtual switches. Writes
one resource each and never mutates.

No arguments.

#### `start`

Start a VM. No-op if already running; verifies by reading the state back rather
than trusting the cmdlet's exit.

| argument | type   | required | default | description                         |
| -------- | ------ | -------- | ------- | ----------------------------------- |
| `vmName` | string | yes      |         | Name of the target virtual machine. |

#### `stop`

Stop a VM. Graceful by default, which needs the guest's Shutdown integration
service responding. force cuts power instead and risks the guest filesystem; it
warns when used.

| argument | type    | required | default | description                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| -------- | ------- | -------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmName` | string  | yes      |         |                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| `force`  | boolean | no       | `false` | Cut power instead of asking the guest to shut down. A graceful stop needs the Shutdown integration service responding; force does not, and risks the guest filesystem exactly as pulling the plug would. |

#### `checkpoint`

Take a checkpoint. Verifies the checkpoint actually appeared afterwards -- a
zero exit is not proof it exists.

| argument | type   | required | default | description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| -------- | ------ | -------- | ------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmName` | string | yes      |         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `name`   | string | yes      |         | Checkpoint name to create. Must not already exist on this VM: the method refuses a duplicate rather than letting Hyper-V decide what to do about the collision, because the caller would not then know which restore point they ended up with. |

#### `restoreCheckpoint`

Roll a VM back to a checkpoint. DESTRUCTIVE: everything since that checkpoint is
discarded, silently and with no undo, so confirmDiscardSince must repeat the
checkpoint name.

| argument              | type   | required | default | description                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| --------------------- | ------ | -------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmName`              | string | yes      |         |                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `name`                | string | yes      |         | Checkpoint to roll back to.                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `confirmDiscardSince` | string | yes      |         | Must equal the checkpoint name. Restoring discards every change made since it was taken, and that loss is silent -- Hyper-V does not warn and there is no undo. Naming it again is the acknowledgement. |

#### `removeCheckpoint`

Delete a checkpoint, merging its differencing disk. Does not change the running
state of the VM.

| argument | type   | required | default | description                                                                                     |
| -------- | ------ | -------- | ------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmName` | string | yes      |         |                                                                                                 |
| `name`   | string | yes      |         | Checkpoint to remove. Must already exist on this VM; it is the checkpoint that will be deleted. |

#### `delete`

Delete a VM. DESTRUCTIVE: confirmName must exactly equal vmName. Disks are LEFT
IN PLACE unless deleteDisks is set, matching Hyper-V's own default rather than
being harsher than it.

| argument               | type    | required | default | description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ---------------------- | ------- | -------- | ------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmName`               | string  | yes      |         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `confirmName`          | string  | yes      |         | Must exactly equal vmName. Deleting removes the machine and its checkpoints; a vmName arriving from a workflow input is not something to take on trust.                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `confirmForcePowerOff` | boolean | no       | `false` | Required when the VM is RUNNING. Deleting a running machine cuts its power -- there is no graceful shutdown in this path and the guest filesystem takes the same risk as pulling the plug. Deletion of a running VM is refused unless this is set, so the power-off is a decision rather than a side effect of the delete. |
| `deleteDisks`          | boolean | no       | `false` | Also delete the VHDX files. Off by default: Hyper-V's own Remove-VM leaves disks behind, and silently destroying them would be a harsher default than the platform's own.                                                                                                                                                  |

### Data written

| resource     | lifetime | fields                                                                                                 | description                                                                                               |
| ------------ | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `vmHost`     | infinite | `name`, `logicalProcessorCount`, `memoryCapacityBytes`, `virtualMachinePath`, `vmCount`, `switchCount` | The Hyper-V host itself: capacity and where it keeps VMs.                                                 |
| `vm`         | infinite | `name`, `state`, `status`, `generation`, `cpuCount`, `memoryAssignedBytes`, `uptimeSeconds`            | One record per virtual machine. Summary only -- no device contents, no console credentials.               |
| `checkpoint` | infinite | `vmName`, `name`, `checkpointType`, `createdAt`, `parentName`                                          | One record per checkpoint. createdAt is normalised to ISO-8601 from the /Date(ms)/ form PowerShell emits. |
| `vmSwitch`   | infinite | `name`, `switchType`                                                                                   | One record per virtual switch, with its type resolved from the numeric form PowerShell returns.           |

## Example

```yaml
globalArguments:
  # Source both from a vault so no machine identity lands in a tracked file.
  host: ${{ vault.get(<your-vault>, <your-host-address-item>) }}
  user: ${{ vault.get(<your-vault>, <your-host-user-item>) }}
  port: 22
  timeoutSec: 30
```

## Caveats

**Authentication is public-key only, and left to ssh.** Load an identity the
target authorizes before running anything here — from an agent, or from your own
ssh configuration. This model handles no key material and takes no password
argument, and it restricts ssh to public-key authentication so a host offering
passwords or keyboard-interactive cannot be used as a fallback. It does not
claim to control which identity files ssh loads; that remains yours to
configure.

**The Windows sshd's default shell is `cmd.exe`.** Anything with a quote, pipe,
or brace gets mangled twice before PowerShell ever sees it, so commands are sent
with `-EncodedCommand` as base64 UTF-16LE. This is not premature: a literal pipe
in a remote command has already truncated a script and left a file half-written.

**.NET serialisation traps.** VM `State` is an enum that serialises as its
NUMBER, so a stopped VM arrives as `3` rather than `"Off"`; it is resolved
host-side with `ToString()` rather than against an enum table here that would
drift as Microsoft adds values. `CreationTime` arrives as
`/Date(1234567890000)/` and is converted in TypeScript, where the accepted forms
are validated rather than softened — a value that is neither the .NET form nor
ISO-8601 is rejected, not stored as "no timestamp". Both parse cleanly into
something wrong if taken at face value, which is the dangerous kind of wrong.

(Hyper-V's `SecureBoot` has the same shape — an enum where **0 means ON**, so
reading it as a boolean reports the security posture backwards. This extension
does not collect it. Worth knowing if you extend the model.)

`ConvertTo-Json` returns an object for one item and an array for many, so the
remote side is always told to emit an array. Code that assumes one shape breaks
the first time the count changes.

## Security

**Transport.** SSH to the host's OpenSSH server, authenticated by whatever
identity ssh selects — an agent identity, or an identity file your own ssh
configuration names or defaults to. This model narrows ssh to public-key
authentication but does not choose the key; that remains yours to configure, and
it is listed as an operator decision below rather than a guarantee. No
credential is read, stored, or accepted as an argument.

**What is written.** Summaries only: names, states, capacity, switch types,
checkpoint names and timestamps. No device contents, no console credentials, no
guest filesystem data.

**What the identifiers themselves reveal.** Resource IDs are not opaque. Each is
built as `<kind>--<target>--<name>[--<name>]-<sha256>`, where `<target>` is the
slugged `user@host:port` you configured — **including the login user**, which is
therefore readable in every resource ID. The user is part of identity because
Hyper-V shows an unprivileged account a subset of what a privileged one sees, so
two configurations differing only by account see different inventories and must
not overwrite each other. It is the reported machine name that is deliberately
_not_ used, since two machines can answer to one hostname and would then share
IDs. The remaining readable parts are lowercase-slugged VM, switch or checkpoint
names; checkpoints carry two, the VM and the checkpoint. The host record is
`vmhost--<target>--<reported-name>-<sha256>`: scoped by the target like
everything else, with the name the host reports about itself as its subject. The
digest exists to prevent collisions, not to conceal: anyone who can list
resource IDs can read your host and VM names out of them. Tags carry inventory
too: checkpoint resources have a `vm` tag holding the VM name, VM resources have
a `state` tag, and the host resource has a `vmCount` tag. Tags are a queryable
index rather than an opaque field, so they are part of this exposure and not a
footnote to it. This is deliberate — IDs that cannot be read are IDs nobody can
operate on — but it means the ID namespace is part of the inventory exposure
described below, not a way around it.

**What mutates, and what stops it.** `start` and `stop` change run state;
`stop --force` cuts power and risks the guest filesystem exactly as pulling the
plug would, and says so when used. `checkpoint` and `removeCheckpoint` add and
drop restore points. Two methods can destroy work that cannot be recovered, and
both require an explicit acknowledgement that repeats the target's name:

- `delete` removes the machine and its checkpoints, and needs `confirmName` to
  equal `vmName` exactly. `deleteDisks` is off by default, because Hyper-V's own
  `Remove-VM` leaves disks behind and destroying them silently would be harsher
  than the platform's own default.
- `restoreCheckpoint` discards every change made since the checkpoint was taken.
  That loss is silent — Hyper-V does not warn and there is no undo — so
  `confirmDiscardSince` must repeat the checkpoint name.
- Deleting a **running** VM cuts its power: this path has no graceful shutdown,
  and the guest filesystem takes the same risk as pulling the plug. It is
  refused unless `confirmForcePowerOff` is set, so the power cut is a decision
  rather than a side effect of the delete.

When `deleteDisks` is used, each file is removed and then verified absent, and
any disk that survives fails the method. Failures are reported by position,
never by path — a disk path names a volume layout and usually the VM, and these
messages reach logs and stored resources.

The point of both guards is a `vmName` arriving from a workflow input: it should
fail rather than succeed against the wrong machine.

**Caller-supplied names appear in errors and logs; remote output does not.** A
message like `no VM named <your-vm-name>` names infrastructure deliberately. The
distinction is provenance: remote output is screened hard — stderr is reduced to
a fixed verdict, malformed stdout is reported as a byte count, and parse
failures name the field rather than the value — because none of it was chosen by
you. A VM name you passed in is already in your workflow definition, already a
resource field, already a tag, and already readable inside the resource ID.
Redacting it from an error while writing it to the record beside that error
protects nothing and makes a destructive method undiagnosable. If that trade is
wrong for your environment, the resource records are the thing to reconsider,
not the error text.

**Shared disks are refused, but the check cannot be atomic.** `deleteDisks` will
not remove a VHDX that is attached to another VM — a shared disk, a differencing
chain, or the same file added twice — because deleting one VM would otherwise
destroy storage another machine is still using. Ownership is checked before
`Remove-VM` runs (afterwards the attachment information no longer exists) and
re-checked immediately before each file is removed, with paths normalised so two
spellings of one file are not treated as two files. A residual window remains:
another VM can attach a disk between the last check and the delete. Over SSH
that window can be narrowed, not closed, and it is stated here rather than
papered over.

**Names must identify one object.** PowerShell's `-Name` parameters accept
wildcards, so `*` is a well-formed argument that means _every_ machine. Every
name this model accepts is refused if it contains `*`, `?`, `[` or `]`, along
with control characters and surrounding whitespace. Without that, the
confirmation guards above would be satisfiable by passing a wildcard twice —
which confirms nothing, on every VM at once.

**Verification, not exit codes.** `start`, `stop`, and `checkpoint` read the
resulting state back rather than trusting the cmdlet's exit status, and the
responses are parsed against declared schemas rather than cast. A required field
that is absent, or a collection that is missing rather than empty, is an error —
not "zero found". `delete` reconciles the disk-removal results against the
number of disks the host reported, because a proof that went missing is not a
proof of success.

See [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/jpisgeek/slog-bog/blob/main/SECURITY.md)
for the release gates every version passes before it reaches the registry.
